chapter.title: Lackey: an example tool
chapter.para: To use this tool, you must specify --tool=lackey on the Valgrind command line.

sect1.title: Overview
sect1.para: Lackey is a simple Valgrind tool that does various kinds of basic program measurement. It adds quite a lot of simple instrumentation to the program's code. It is primarily intended to be of use as an example tool, and consequently emphasises clarity of implementation over performance.

listitem.para: When enabled, Lackey prints the following statistics and information about the execution of the client program:
The number of calls to the function specified by the --fnname option (the default is main). If the program has had its symbols stripped, the count will always be zero.
The number of conditional branches encountered and the number and proportion of those taken.
The number of superblocks entered and completed by the program. Note that due to optimisations done by the JIT, this is not at all an accurate value.
The number of guest (x86, amd64, ppc, etc.) instructions and IR statements executed. IR is Valgrind's RISC-like intermediate representation via which all instrumentation is done.
Ratios between some of these counts.
The exit code of the client program.

When enabled, Lackey prints a table containing counts of loads, stores and ALU operations, differentiated by their IR types. The IR types are identified by their IR name ("I1", "I8", ... "I128", "F32", "F64", and "V128").

When enabled, Lackey prints the size and address of almost every memory access made by the program. See the comments at the top of the file lackey/lk_main.c for details about the output format, how it works, and inaccuracies in the address trace. Note that this option produces immense amounts of output.

When enabled, Lackey prints out the address of every superblock (a single entry, multiple exit, linear chunk of code) executed by the program. This is primarily of interest to Valgrind developers. See the comments at the top of the file lackey/lk_main.c for details about the output format. Note that this option produces large amounts of output.
Changes the function for which calls are counted when --basic-counts=yes is specified.
Controls whether Lackey instruments code at startup. When disabled, Lackey adds no counting or tracing helpers. Instrumentation can be enabled later with the client requests described below.

Include instructions whose function name matches the pattern. This option can be repeated. Patterns use Valgrind's * and ? wildcards and match demangled function names. With --read-inline-info=yes, matching any function in the instruction's inline call chain includes that instruction. Without this option, only the containing non-inlined function is available. Instructions with no matching function information are excluded when a function filter is present.

Include instructions whose source filename matches the pattern. Patterns are checked against the filename, its basename, and the directory plus filename recorded in debug information. This option can be repeated. Files are source files, not executable or shared-library names. Compile with debug information to provide source locations; instructions without a source location are excluded when a file filter is present.

Append instruction, memory, and superblock trace records to a dedicated file. The special value log selects the ordinary Valgrind log; use ./log for a file with that name. File paths are used literally, without percent substitutions. Counters, diagnostics, and monitor replies remain on the Valgrind log. Dedicated trace output is buffered and flushed when switching output, disabling instrumentation, printing status, before fork or exec, and at exit. Buffered data can be lost on abrupt termination such as SIGKILL.

sect1.title: Runtime control and instruction selection
sect1.para: With no filters and instrumentation enabled, Lackey retains its usual behavior. Multiple function patterns are alternatives, as are multiple file patterns. If both categories are present, an instruction must satisfy both. Clearing a category removes its restriction. Selection is evaluated at each guest instruction during translation, including instructions reached by Valgrind's superblock chaining. Excluded instructions receive no Lackey helpers. Selecting a function does not automatically include functions it calls. A file match uses the instruction's line-table source location, not every file in its inline call chain. JIT code without registered function or source information cannot match the corresponding filters.

All Lackey modes use the selection. With filters, a superblock is counted and its trace entry emitted when its first included instruction is reached. The SB record gives that instruction's address. A completed superblock is counted only when its last instruction is included. Instruction and IR counts cover included instructions. Empty selections and runs that never enable instrumentation are valid and produce zero counts.
The following monitor commands can be issued from GDB, via vgdb, or from the client program with VALGRIND_MONITOR_COMMAND:
sect1.programlisting: lackey instrumentation on lackey instrumentation off lackey function add <glob> lackey function clear lackey file add <glob> lackey file clear lackey filters clear lackey output <path> lackey output log lackey status
sect1.para: A pattern or path occupies the remainder of the command, including spaces; do not add shell-style quotes inside the command string. Instrumentation changes and filter changes discard cached translations, so previously executed code follows the new selection on its next execution. The settings are global to the process and apply to all threads. A multi-command configuration update is not atomic: disable instrumentation first when changing several settings. These commands do not reset accumulated counters.

Lackey also accepts CALLGRIND_START_INSTRUMENTATION and CALLGRIND_STOP_INSTRUMENTATION from callgrind/callgrind.h as aliases. Other Callgrind requests, including toggling collection and dumping statistics, are not implemented by Lackey. VALGRIND_CLO_CHANGE does not replace these monitor commands: the ordinary option callback does not permit the translation invalidation required for safe switching.

Rust's monitor_command returns true when a command succeeds; the C VALGRIND_MONITOR_COMMAND returns zero. Check these results to detect an unsupported Valgrind build or a failed output switch. An invalid command leaves settings unchanged. A failed file open keeps the previous output sink and returns failure. An unrecoverable write failure terminates the process with an error, rather than silently dropping trace records. Valgrind's protected-descriptor allocation is also fatal if its descriptor reserve is exhausted.

Output switches open the next file before closing the previous one. Files are always appended, so switching A to B and back to A preserves both A regions. This supports output contexts whose exit restores the previous path. A fork flushes pending records first; parent and child then append to the inherited file unless either switches output. Their subsequent records may interleave and contain no process or thread identifiers. A context that changes global instrumentation or output must coordinate with other threads. Pending records are also flushed before exec, which otherwise replaces the tool state without running its normal exit handler.
